Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:11: Besides the fact that whoever converses in idle words is called a mocker, he transgresses a positive commandment, as it is said, "and you shall speak of them" (Deuteronomy 6:7). And so in tractate Yoma, first chapter (19b), in these words: our Rabbis taught, "and you shall speak of them" — and not in prayer [with idle talk mixed in]. "Of them" — you have permission to speak, but not of other things. "And you shall speak of them" — make them fixed. Rava said, whoever converses in mundane talk transgresses a positive commandment, as it is said, "and you shall speak of them," and not of other things. Rav Acha bar Yaakov said, he transgresses a negative commandment, as it is said, "all things are wearisome, man cannot express it" (Ecclesiastes 1:8) — so far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:12: Particularly students of Torah must be very careful of idle words, as they say in the Midrash Shir HaShirim (Rabbah 1:21), on the verse (1:3), "because of the fragrance of your good oils": just as with oil, a full cup does not spill over when mixed with other liquids, so words of Torah do not spill over into words of mockery. Just as, if you have a full cup of oil in your hand and a drop of water falls into it, a drop of oil comes out to match it — so if a word of Torah enters the heart, a word of mockery comes out to match it; and if a word of mockery enters the heart, a word of Torah comes out to match it — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:13: Included in this class is the class of those who play dice and other kinds of games; even if they do not play to win money from one another, which would involve theft, there is still the matter of "two who sit together with no words of Torah between them, this is a session of mockers," as explained. This is comparable to the kinds of games mentioned in tractate Avodah Zarah (18b), which they say are a "session of mockers," in these words: our Rabbis taught, whoever goes to the stadiums or circuses, and sees there the snake charmers, the buffoons, the clowns, the acrobats, the jugglers, the masked performers, the disguised ones — this is a session of mockers, and concerning them the verse says, "who has not walked [in the counsel of the wicked]... but his desire is in the Torah of the Lord" (Psalms 1:1-2) — you thus learn that these things bring a person to the neglect of Torah — so far his words. Rashi explains: these are kinds of mockery — you thus learn, from the juxtaposition of "but in the Torah of the Lord," that whoever goes to these does not have his desire in the Torah of the Lord — so far his words. This makes it explicit that since he is idle from the Torah of the Lord through these kinds of games, they are called a session of mockers, and the same applies to other kinds of games.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:14: There are those who have permitted for themselves kinds of dice games, saying that it is a thing that sharpens the intellect, and I have seen fit to expose their error, so that they not grow clever with excuses of their inclination against the Torah of the Lord. First, Rabbeinu Yonah wrote in Sefer HaYirah that one who speaks idle words is like one who denies the fundamental principle [of faith] — that he does not believe that the whole earth is full of His glory; for one who believes that he stands before the King, blessed and exalted be He, would not do anything against His will. In my eyes this matter is harder than all other transgressions — for with all other transgressions, if the sinner sins momentarily, his inclination suddenly deceived him and he did not place the fear of the Lord before him, his punishment is not so great; but this one, who with a haughty soul sits for an hour or three hours, and sometimes the whole day, does not remember the Lord before him, and does not say in his heart, "Before whom do I stand and play, stand and provoke," and is not ashamed of His greatness nor afraid of His judgment, and transgresses the negative commandment "take heed to yourself lest you forget the Lord your God," and forgets the Lord, and yet sits and plays — behold, he deliberately demeans the Lord and His Torah, saying in his heart that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not punish the class of mockers — he thereby denies the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, and is like a Sadducee. He is similar to those about whom the Holy One, blessed be He, complained to the prophet Ezekiel, who worshiped idols in secret and said, "the Lord has forsaken the land, the Lord does not see us" (Ezekiel 8:12) — and these worship idols in purity, meaning, they give an excuse as if it were permitted to do it openly, with no one to protest against them. And if our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Nedarim 22b) of one who is angry, that the Shechinah is not considered important to him, all the more so would they say of this class, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:15: Further, we find in the Gemara (Niddah 13a) regarding one who holds his organ and urinates, that they said to Rabbi Eliezer that it appeared like one whose organ was cut, casting an aspersion on his children as though they were illegitimate, and he answered: better that he cast an aspersion on his children as though they were illegitimate, than that he make himself wicked before the Omnipresent for even a single hour. Accordingly, all the more so one who plays dice, making himself wicked before the Omnipresent for more than two hours, and possibly a whole day — this argument is a matter of plain reason.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:16: Further, in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, they say in tractate Bava Batra (79a): Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, whoever separates himself from words of Torah and occupies himself with idle talk, fire consumes him, as it is said, "and I have set My face against them; they shall go forth from the fire, and the fire shall devour them" (Ezekiel 15:7). Further there: when Ravin came, he said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, whoever lets himself go slack from words of Torah falls into Gehinnom, as it is said, "a man who strays from the way of understanding shall rest in the assembly of the shades (refa'im)" (Proverbs 21:16), and "refa'im" refers only to those who descend to Gehinnom, as it is said, "and he does not know that the shades are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol" (Proverbs 9:18) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:17: Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, peace be upon him, wrote in the book Menorat HaMa'or (letter 31), in these words: and one who occupies himself with idle words, even though there is no forbidden speech in them, wastes the time that he could have occupied with words of Torah to acquire the life of the World to Come; and it appears from his mind that he demeans, in his own eyes, the words of God and the reward of the World to Come — as we learn in the chapter Chelek (99a): it was taught, Rabbi Meir says, whoever learns Torah and does not teach it, this is [what is meant by] "for he has despised the word of the Lord"; Rabbi Nehorai says, whoever is able to occupy himself with Torah and does not — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:18: Not only that, but even one who is able to occupy himself with Torah and does not wish to, even if he does not speak words of mockery, his session is called a session of mockers, as we learn in chapter 3 of Avot: two who sit together with no words of Torah between them, this is a session of mockers, and so on. Not only does he sin against his own soul and lose the life of the World to Come and inherit Gehinnom, but he also causes many others to sin — for in occupying himself with idle talk, he draws the hearts of many to be idle together with him, and their sin is dependent on him — as we learn in chapter 5 of Avot: Jeroboam sinned and caused the many to sin, the sin of the many is dependent on him, as it is said, "for the sins of Jeroboam which he sinned, and which he caused Israel to sin" (II Kings 13:2). He is also punished in that they do not enable him to repent, and there is no greater punishment than this, as we learn in the chapter Yom HaKippurim (Yoma 87a): whoever confers merit upon the many, no sin comes about through him; and whoever causes the many to sin, they do not enable him to repent — so far his words, as pertains to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:19: Let no one say, "Who can be careful to keep all the words of our Rabbis? I will be careful now regarding this one, and since I am not careful regarding the others, I will not be careful regarding this one either." This argument too is rejected, for "one transgression draws another" (Avot 4:2), and if he is not careful of this one, his inclination will lead him to sin in all four classes that do not see the presence of the Shechinah, so that he will be excluded from the World to Come — and woe to one who says with his mouth that he does not want to see the presence of the Shechinah, in order to fulfill the desire of his inclination and be among the class of mockers and the other classes! But if he sanctifies himself in this one, "whoever comes to purify himself, they assist him" (Yoma 38b), and he will not sin in the other classes and will be saved from them, as they said, of blessed memory (Yoma 39a), "if a person sanctifies himself a little, they sanctify him a great deal."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:20: Those who play dice and other kinds of games on festivals and holidays — woe to their souls, for they have done themselves harm! For the days of the festivals are days of judgment, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, say (Rosh Hashanah 1:1): at four times the world is judged — on Passover, regarding grain; on Shavuot (Atzeret), regarding the fruit of the tree; on Rosh Hashanah, all who come into the world pass before Him like a flock of sheep; on Sukkot (the festival), they are judged regarding water. This shows that all the festivals are days of judgment, and therefore they said (Yerushalmi Shabbat 15:3) that Sabbaths and festivals were given to Israel only so that they might occupy themselves with Torah. And they said (Kiddushin 40b): a person should always view himself and the world as though half meritorious and half guilty — if he does a mitzvah, he tips himself and the whole world to the scale of merit, and if not, God forbid, he tips it to the scale of guilt. It follows that one who sins then, with playing and levity, is more severe than at any other time of the year, since, given that the world is in judgment, one sin could tip the whole world to the scale of guilt — and then all those poor people who will die or suffer from hunger and thirst are all dependent on him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:21: On the days of the festivals, besides the fact that people's sustenance is at stake, people's lives and souls are also at stake in the judgment, and so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains this Mishnah that we quoted (Zohar Parashat Vayechi 226b), that it entirely speaks of the souls being judged — see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:22: Therefore it is fitting to distance oneself from all kinds of games, whether on weekdays or on the days of the festivals, for the world and man are always in judgment, as we quoted from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him (Parashat Vayechi 226b-227a) and the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Rosh Hashanah 16a) in the Gate of Awe, chapter 11. This sin causes sufferings and destruction to the world, according to the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Avodah Zarah 18b); therefore one must be careful not to stumble again, and his repentance will be accepted, please God.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:23: It appears that all those interpretations stated there (Sanhedrin 99a) explaining the verse "for he has despised the word of the Lord" are all included in mockery, for the mocker is one who demeans matters, as we have said. It says there: "for he has despised the word of the Lord" (Numbers 15:31) — this refers to one who says the Torah is not from Heaven. Another interpretation: this refers to an apostate (apikoros). "And has broken His commandment" — this refers to one who breaks the covenant of the flesh [circumcision]. It was taught in another [Baraita]: "for he has despised the word of the Lord" — this refers to one who says the Torah is not from Heaven; and even if he said the Torah is from Heaven, except for this one verse, saying that the Holy One, blessed be He, did not say it, but that Moses said it on his own accord — this is [called] "despising the word of the Lord"; and even if he said the whole Torah is from Heaven, except for this fine point, this a fortiori argument, this verbal analogy — this too is "for he has despised the word of the Lord." It was taught: Rabbi Meir used to say, whoever learns Torah and does not teach it, this is "for he has despised the word of the Lord." Rabbi Natan says, whoever does not pay attention to the Mishnah. Rabbi Nechemiah says, and so on — so far his words, as pertains to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:24: Just as we are obligated to believe in the whole Torah of Moses, so we are obligated to believe in all the words of the Sages, and what is said in the Midrashim and the Aggadot. Even though something may appear to be beyond nature, we should attribute the shortcoming to our own limited understanding, and not to their statement. Whoever mocks any of their statements is punished, as we say in the chapter Osin Pasin (Eruvin 21b): Rav Pappa said in the name of Rabbah bar Ulla, whoever mocks the words of the Sages is judged with boiling excrement; and so they say in Gittin (57a); and so we find that a certain student was punished for mocking the words of Rabbi Yochanan, who said the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to bring precious stones thirty by thirty cubits, and so on, as is stated in Bava Batra (75a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:25: Regarding the punishment of the class of flatterers, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, say in the chapter Arvei Pesachim (113b) that there are three the Holy One, blessed be He, hates: one who speaks one thing with his mouth and another in his heart — this being the trait of flattery; one who knows testimony for his fellow and does not testify for him; and one who sees nakedness in his fellow and testifies against him alone [without a second witness].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:26: We learn in Sanhedrin (52a): Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, what is [the meaning of] "With the flattery of ungodly mockers of a feast, gnashing at me their teeth" (Psalms 35:16)? Because of the flattery Korah's assembly showed him regarding matters of eating, the Prince of Gehinnom gnashed his teeth at them. In the chapter Elu Ne'emarin (Sotah 41b): Rabbi Elazar said, any person who has flattery in him falls into Gehinnom, as it is said, "Woe to those who call evil good..." (Isaiah 5:20), and it is written after it, "therefore, as the fire devours the stubble, and the flame consumes the chaff, so their root shall be as rottenness..." (Isaiah 5:24). Rabbi Elazar said, whoever flatters his fellow eventually falls into his hand, or into the hand of his son, or into the hand of his grandson — from where? From Chananiah ben Azzur, the false prophet, who led Israel astray, and the prophet Jeremiah said, "Amen, may the Lord do so, may the Lord fulfill your words" (Jeremiah 28:6) — and because he did not protest against him, but said, "May the Lord fulfill your words," he fell into the hand of his grandson, as it is said, "and it came to pass, that when he was in the gate of Benjamin, a captain of the ward was there, whose name was Irijah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Chananiah..." (Jeremiah 37:13), and the officers were angry at Jeremiah and put him in prison. And any assembly that has flattery in it is repugnant like a niddah, as it is said, "for the assembly of the flatterer (chanef) is desolate" (Job 15:34), and in the coastal towns they call a niddah "desolate."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:27: And in the Midrash they said: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta [said], from the day the fist of flattery grew strong, judgments became perverted and deeds corrupted, and no man could say to his fellow, "my deeds are greater than yours." Even Jehoshaphat deserved to be judged because he flattered Ahab — and where did he flatter him? As it is said, "and the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, There is yet one man to inquire of the Lord through him, but I hate him..." (I Kings 22:8), and Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so" — and because he did not reproach him sharply, but only said, "Let not the king say so," the prophet said to him, "Should you help the wicked..." (II Chronicles 19:2).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:28: And in Midrash Mishlei (parasha 26), on the verse, "as a stone bound in a sling, so is he who gives honor to a fool" (Proverbs 26:8): Rabbi Alexandri said, whoever gives honor to a fool is like one who throws a stone to Merkolis [an idol] — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:29: This evil trait is more disgraceful in a Torah scholar than in the rest of the people, as it is said, "for both prophet and priest are flatterers" (Jeremiah 23:11), and they say in tractate Yoma (72b): Rabbah said, any Torah scholar whose inside is not like his outside is not called a scholar, as it is said, "within and without shall you overlay it" (Exodus 25:11). Abaye said, he is called an abomination, as it is said, "how much more abominable and corrupt is man..." (Job 15:16).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:30: And they say in Chagigah and Sotah (41b) that the enemies of Israel became liable to destruction because they flattered King Agrippa, even though he was a king, humble and fearing Heaven — all the more so one who flatters the wicked. Rabbi Elazar said, any person who has flattery in him brings wrath into the world, as it is said, "and the flatterers of heart bring wrath" (Job 36:13); and not only that, but his prayer is repugnant, as it is said, "they do not cry out when He binds them" (Job 36:13) — Rashi, of blessed memory, explains: when sufferings come upon them, crying out will not help them; and it is written, "for what is the hope of the flatterer, when he is cut off" (Job 27:8), and it is written, "will God hear his cry when trouble comes upon him?" (Job 27:9). Further they say there: Rabbi Elazar said, any person who has flattery in him, even the fetuses in their mothers' wombs curse him, as it is said, "he who says to the wicked, You are righteous, peoples shall curse him, nations shall despise him" (Proverbs 24:24); and "yiqvuhu" ("shall curse him") means nothing other than a curse, as it is said, "How shall I curse (ekov) whom God has not cursed (kabo)" (Numbers 23:8); and "le'umim" ("nations") means nothing other than fetuses, as it is said, "and one people (le'om) shall be stronger than the other people (le'om)" (Genesis 25:23).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:31: Further, they say in Midrash Mishlei (12:21): "No evil shall befall the righteous, but the wicked are filled with evil" — when he walks in his innocence; "but the wicked are filled with evil" — this refers to one who speaks one thing with his mouth and another in his heart, and the Holy One, blessed be He, calls him an abomination, as it is said, "lying lips are an abomination to the Lord" (Proverbs 12:22). "But they who deal faithfully are His delight" — this refers to one who does business faithfully — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:32: Because of the sin of flattery, people fall into the hands of their enemies and are plundered, as it is said, "Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger... I will send him against a flattering nation..." (Isaiah 10:5-6). And because of the sin of flattery, the Holy One, blessed be He, pours out His wrath on the land, and His hand is stretched out over the young men and orphans and widows, as it is said, "therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men... for everyone is a flatterer and an evildoer..." (Isaiah 9:16).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:33: Flattery is harsh — it is equal to idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed. [Equal to] idolatry — where do we know this? As it is written, "to practice flattery, to speak error against the Lord" (Isaiah 32:6), and "error" (to'eh) refers only to idolatry, as it is said, "they are vanity, a work of errors (ta'tu'im)" (Jeremiah 10:15). [Equal to] forbidden relations — from where? As it is said, "behold, if a man sends away his wife... shall not that land be greatly flattered (chanof technaf)" (Jeremiah 3:1). [Equal to] bloodshed — from where? As it is written, "and the land was flattered (vatechenaf) with blood" (Psalms 106:38).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:34: And because of the sin of flattery, the rains are withheld, as it is said, "and you have flattered the land with your harlotries..." (Jeremiah 3:2), and it is written after it, "therefore the showers have been withheld..." And because of the sin of flattery, the person who commits it in this world is judged in Gehinnom forever and ever, as it is said, "the sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the flatterers: who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire..." (Isaiah 33:14).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:35: In Sotah (41b): Rabbi Yehudah bar Ma'arvia said, and some say Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi: it is permitted to flatter the wicked in this world, as it is said, "the vile person shall no more be called generous, nor the miser said to be bountiful" (Isaiah 32:5) — implying that in this world it is permitted [to call them so]. Reish Lakish said, from here: "as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me" (Genesis 33:10, said by Jacob to Esau). This disagrees with Rabbi Levi, who said, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:36: Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, author of Menorat HaMa'or (letter 45), wrote, in these words: all this does not mean that one should praise the evil traits he practices, for regarding this they already said there are several sins involved; but what it says, "it is permitted to flatter," means that even though it is forbidden to honor the wicked, since they are enemies of the Name — as it is written, "in whose eyes a vile person is despised" (Psalms 15:4) — meaning that it is fitting for one who dwells in the tent of the Lord and abides on His holy mountain to despise one who is despicable in the eyes of the Lord, this being the wicked one, and to honor those who fear the Lord but not the wicked — nevertheless the sage said that the wicked, whose hand is strong and whose time favors them, may be honored out of fear of them, as with men of power, but not out of love for them. And so they say in Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer (ch. 36) regarding Jacob's flattering Esau: from here they said, one may flatter the wicked in this world, for the sake of the ways of peace, and your mnemonic is Mem-Aleph-Heh-Bet-Heh ("ahavah," love), the initial letters of "machnifin et haresha'im ba'olam hazeh" ("they flatter the wicked in this world") — meaning that the mnemonic is "out of love," so that he may live to fulfill the commandments of his Creator. But whoever has the ability to protest and does protest, and takes vengeance from the wicked in this world — the Holy One, blessed be He, makes a covenant with him and with his descendants after him, as He did with Pinchas.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:37: Further, regarding the punishment of the flatterer, they said, of blessed memory (Avot D'Rabbi Natan 29:4): whoever flatters his fellow for the sake of honor eventually is separated from him easily. Similarly, the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot writes (Gate of Sincerity in Deeds, ch. 5), regarding one argument of the evil inclination: the inclination says that a person should do things that people will know of, in order to gain a reputation for piety, so that they learn from his deeds. He answers that one should say to it: perhaps, when I direct my deeds toward this, I will not attain the intended goal through them, and people will think that I am a flatterer in my deeds, and my deeds will be in vain, since my intention in them was not [directed] to God alone. And it is like [the story] told of a certain king: "Why does the reading of so-and-so not please you, though his voice is pleasant and he is skilled in the cantillation of reading?" He said to them, "How could his reading please me, when he does not read it except so that his reading please me and he find favor in my eyes because of it? But if his intention had been only for the will of the Creator, it would have pleased me." And so it is said of anyone, whether among those praying in the congregation or those who compose new liturgical poems, who intends thereby to find favor in people's eyes rather than [only] God's, blessed be He — it is not accepted before the Creator — so far his words. It follows that included in the class of flatterers is one who performs an act of a commandment for God, blessed be He, with the intention that people honor him for it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:38: He writes in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Sincerity in Deeds, ch. 4) that one who does a deed for the honor of people, or out of fear of them, does not serve the Creator but people, and it follows that he does not recognize the Creator; and so it is with the idol worshiper, who worships idols only out of his folly, not having recognized the Creator. He writes, in these words: and the idol worshiper has an advantage over the flatterer in four things. First, the idol worshiper in this time is not warned by a prophet who would clarify to him the corruption of his thinking through signs and wonders, whereas the flatterer within the Torah has arguments against him from what he has received of the commandments in the service of God and the warning against serving another. Second, the idol worshiper serves one who does not rebel against God, but the flatterer serves one who rebels against God, along with one who does not rebel against Him. Third, the idol worshiper serves one thing, whereas for the flatterer there is no end to those he serves [flatters]. Fourth, the idol worshiper's matter is not hidden from people, and they guard themselves against him because of the openness of his denial of God, but the flatterer's denial is not apparent, and people trust him, and he is able to harm them in ways others cannot, and he is the greatest of the world's ailments, and in our language he is called a flatterer, arrogant, and enticer — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:39: Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in the Midrash (Yalkut Mishlei, remez 961): Rabbi Chiya taught, they publicize the flatterers because of the desecration of the Name, as it is said, "his wickedness shall be revealed in the assembly" (Proverbs 26:26), and it says, "and when the righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will lay a stumbling block before him" (Ezekiel 3:20). And why does the Holy One, blessed be He, give them evil? In order to publicize their deeds to the creatures, so that nothing happen to him because of his transgressions and people cry out against the attribute of judgment. Go and learn from Doeg, who was the head of the Sanhedrin, as it is said, "the chief of the herdsmen who belonged to Saul" (I Samuel 21:8), and because he had the trait of evil speech, the verse publicized him — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:40: In the book Menorat HaMa'or, Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, wrote, in these words: the flatterer is more disgraceful than the thief, for the thief steals money, while the flatterer steals people's minds. Flatterers divide into three classes. The first class are those who flatter people in order to find favor in their eyes, and do not reprove them for their evil deeds, but say, "you are acting rightly," even though they are doing evil deeds and unjustly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:41: The second class is more disgraceful than the first — these are those who flatter the powerful and the wealthy, subjugating their souls to them. To the powerful, so that they become heads over the community and inherit positions of authority, and they strive to be honored through the flattery [they show]. To the wealthy, so that they plunder their money and benefit from it, and they remove their confidence from the Holy One, blessed be He, and place their hope and expectation in people, thinking that their money will never end and will never be lost from their hands — in this they err, and concerning them it is said, "cursed is the man who trusts in man" (Jeremiah 17:5).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:42: The third class is more disgraceful still — these are those who flatter in religion, showing themselves to be righteous, diligent in attending synagogues, but their intent is to rise to greatness so that they be appointed leaders over the community and remove themselves from taxation, showing piety on their faces while their hearts are full of deceit and treachery — so far his words. I have not written some of his words and some of the essence of his wording, because of the length.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:43: Further, Rabbeinu Yonah elaborates at length in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 3, item 187) regarding flatterers, and writes nine divisions regarding them — whoever wishes to see this, his book is available. The sum of his words is that one should not flatter a wicked person, nor speak in his praise, whether in his presence or not in his presence, as it is said, "those who forsake the Torah praise the wicked" (Proverbs 28:4). Similarly, one might speak of one who is appointed leader or sage over the community, when that person is unfit, and the Holy One, blessed be He, punishes the one who appointed him — for that scholar is found to destroy the world through his improper rulings and the like. Included in flattery: if one does not wish to reprove the people of his town, thinking they will not accept it from him, he is called a flatterer — so he writes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:44: I found written in a book speaking of matters of piety, in these words: there are three whom one may flatter — one's wife, for the sake of peace in the home; a creditor, so that he not press him; and one's teacher, so that he may teach him Torah and commandments. And it is a great mitzvah to flatter one's students and colleagues so that they may learn, and so that they heed his words to accept reproof and fulfill the commandments; and likewise anyone he thinks he can draw toward himself so that they heed him to fulfill the commandments — for if he comes to them angrily they will not heed him, but with flattery they will accept his reproof — and this is a great mitzvah, to flatter him, to bring forth the precious from the vile.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:45: There is a person who accepts reproof and rebuke only gently, as it is said, "the words of the wise are heard in quiet" (Ecclesiastes 9:17). And there is one who needs rebuke, as it is said, "a rebuke enters deeper into a person of understanding" (Proverbs 17:10, adapted). And there is one for whom even striking would not help, as it is said, "than to strike a fool a hundred [times]" (Proverbs 17:10, adapted). If so, what should be done? There is no remedy for him — drive him away.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:46: There is a very evil kind of flattery — such as a person who speaks with his fellow and flatters him with sweet words in order to draw him close and get him to say what is in his heart, and after he has come to trust and rely on him, he deals treacherously with him. This is like what is said (Proverbs 1:17), "for in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird," "and they lie in wait for their own blood, they hide for their own lives" (Proverbs 1:18) — for hunters scatter wheat in a net so that the birds come to eat and then are caught; this flatterer is comparable to this.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:47: The Sages forbade flattery, and they said (Chullin 94a) that a person should not send a gift knowing the recipient will not accept it, nor invite his fellow to eat with him knowing he will not eat, and likewise, if a person wants to open a barrel of wine to sell and his fellow comes to buy wine, he should not say to him, "I am opening the barrel for your sake." All this and the like is called "stealing people's minds" — flattering and stealing the minds of people.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:48: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta said: from the day the fist of flattery grew strong, judgments became perverted and deeds corrupted, and no man could say to his fellow, "my deeds are greater than yours." Rabbi Elazar said, whoever has flattery in him brings wrath into the world, as it is said, "and the flatterers of heart bring wrath" (Job 36:13), and his prayer is not heard; even the fetuses in their mothers' wombs curse him in Gehinnom. And whoever flatters a wicked person eventually falls into his hand, and if he does not fall into his own hand, he falls into the hand of his son or the hand of his grandson. And any woman who has flattery in her is repugnant like a niddah, and in the end she is exiled (Sotah 42a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:49: Therefore a person should distance himself from flattery, and should not flatter to encourage another's wickedness; even if he has benefits to receive from him, he should not flatter him; and he should not flatter his relatives or his children when they are not walking in a good path — for many people persist in their wickedness because they see they have no shame regarding their unseemly ways, and because they see people flattering them. There is nothing in the world that locks the gates of repentance like flattery.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:50: There is a story of a certain worthy man who had a daughter to marry off, and there were in his town two young men, each of whom wished to take his daughter. The worthy man went to judge between them in order to test them; he arranged for a certain person to pick a quarrel with him, and eventually they would be brought to be judged between the disputant and himself, in order to test them, and so they did. Of these two, one flattered that worthy man in order to marry his daughter, always finding him in the right in every way; but then he went and gave his daughter to the one who had found him at fault, [saying] "for he is a good man," so said the worthy man, "because he did not flatter me and did not show me favoritism" (Sefer Chasidim, siman 842).
